# Motivation

## Motivation: Why simulate patients?

Robotic assistive devices could improve mobility after neurological injury,
but tuning their controllers takes long, costly human experiments.

::: {.fragment}
- The people who would benefit most are often least able to walk for hours
- Muscle-driven imitation learning (IL): train a policy to reproduce recorded
  walking on a musculoskeletal model, then use the simulation in place of the participant
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
The simulation is only as good as the muscle-level solution the policy finds.
:::

::: notes
~35 s. Set up the promise of simulation-in-the-loop design, then the catch.
:::

## Motivation: Kinematics can match while muscles don't

Healthy-gait benchmark: simulated muscle activation vs. measured EMG [@ahmad2026beyond]

```{=html}
<div class="bench">
  <div class="panel">
    <div class="ptitle">RMSE <span>(lower is better)</span></div>
    <div class="row"><div>HyFyDy</div><div class="track"><div class="bar hyfydy" style="width:41%"></div></div><div class="val">0.164</div></div>
    <div class="row"><div>MuJoCo</div><div class="track"><div class="bar mujoco" style="width:86%"></div></div><div class="val">0.344</div></div>
    <div class="axis"><span>0</span><span>0.2</span><span>0.4</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="panel">
    <div class="ptitle">Correlation r <span>(higher is better)</span></div>
    <div class="row"><div>HyFyDy</div><div class="track"><div class="bar hyfydy" style="width:80%"></div></div><div class="val">0.40</div></div>
    <div class="row"><div>MuJoCo</div><div class="track"><div class="bar mujoco" style="width:22%"></div></div><div class="val">0.11</div></div>
    <div class="axis"><span>0</span><span>0.25</span><span>0.5</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="note">Pooled across muscles.</div>
```

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Both frameworks tracked healthy kinematics, yet differed sharply in EMG fidelity.
Kinematic agreement is a weak indicator of correct muscle activity.
:::

::: notes
~40 s. HyFyDy 0.164 / 0.40 vs MuJoCo 0.344 / 0.11.
:::

## Motivation:The problem with pathological gait

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
[Healthy gait]{.label}

The imitation and effort objectives agree, since healthy walking is close to
metabolically optimal.
:::
::: {.col .fragment fragment-index=1}
[After stroke or incomplete SCI]{.label}

The kinematics come from inefficient neural drive, so the two objectives conflict.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway fragment-index=2}
An effort-minimizing policy tracking patient kinematics may reproduce the joint
angles through a mechanism the patient does not use.
:::

::: notes
~35 s. This is the core risk the project tests.
:::

# Objectives

## Objectives and Hypotheses

Determine whether the wrong muscle solution occurs, how to detect it, and what
prevents it.

::: {.hyp-list}
::: {.hyp .fragment}
[H1]{.hyp-tag} Baseline policies track stroke kinematics but match EMG less closely
than matched able-bodied controls, especially on the paretic side.
:::

::: {.hyp .fragment}
[H2]{.hyp-tag} Synergy constraints improve EMG fidelity over the baseline without a
meaningful loss in kinematic tracking.
:::

::: {.hyp .fragment}
[H3]{.hyp-tag} Scaling the model to body dimensions improves tracking, with a smaller
effect on EMG fidelity than the controller change.
:::
:::

::: notes
~35 s.
:::

# Methodology

## Methodology: 2 × 2 within-participant design

```{=html}
<table class="design">
  <colgroup><col style="width:22%"><col style="width:39%"><col style="width:39%"></colgroup>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th></th>
      <th>Generic model<span>default HyFyDy</span></th>
      <th>Scaled model<span>OpenSim scale factors → HyFyDy</span></th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th>Baseline controller<span>one command per muscle</span></th>
      <td>Existing pipeline, unchanged from the healthy benchmark
        <div class="h">H1: compared with matched controls</div></td>
      <td>Same controller on a body-scaled model
        <div class="h">H3: effect of scaling</div></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th>Synergy controller<span>a few synergy commands</span></th>
      <td>Muscle weights from the participant's own EMG; timing still learned
        <div class="h">H2: effect of the controller</div></td>
      <td>Both changes together
        <div class="h">Controller vs. model effect size</div></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```

Every participant is run in all four conditions. Personalization is geometric only:
it does not model patient-specific weakness, spasticity, or muscle properties.

::: notes
~45 s. Walk across the rows: baseline vs. synergy is H2, generic vs. scaled is H3.
:::

## Methodology: Data, controllers, and evaluation

```{=html}
<ol class="pipeline">
  <li><span>Data</span>Van Criekinge dataset; 5 stroke survivors, 5 matched controls</li>
  <li><span>Split</span>Training and held-out strides, before any synergy extraction</li>
  <li><span>Reference</span>Markers to reference motion; OpenSim scaling to HyFyDy</li>
  <li><span>Train</span>Imitation and effort reward, benchmark settings</li>
  <li><span>Evaluate</span>Simulated activation vs. EMG on held-out strides</li>
</ol>
```

::: {.two-col .small}
::: {.col}
[Synergy controller]{.label}

Non-negative matrix factorization per leg over six leg muscles, using the fewest
synergies that explain at least 90% of EMG variance. The policy still learns
when each group activates.
:::
::: {.col}
[Primary outcome]{.label}

EMG fidelity across the gait cycle, per muscle and per leg, with paretic and
non-paretic legs reported separately. Kinematic tracking is a necessary check,
not evidence of a correct muscle solution.
:::
:::

[Data: [@vancriekinge2023]. Synergy rationale: [@meyer2016synergies; @clark2010merging].]{.src}

::: notes
~40 s. Emphasize held-out strides.
:::
